\chapter{Pointing, and Asking}
\label{ch:sa-pointing-and-asking}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at something in Sanskrit and ask who or where it is — and I can say what the six words have in common.}

Say the near word, the far word and the question word in a row, and name the part that changed.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[etat]{\sk{एतत्} (etat) — this one — the thing near me}

\label{lesson:SA-C14-this}



\begin{quote}
You can already name things. This is how you POINT at them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{एतत्}}
\textbf{\sk{एतत्}} — \emph{etat} — this one — the thing near me.

Say it, and point while you say it. That is the whole word: it does not mean anything on its own, it means whatever your finger is on.

Its partner is \textbf{\sk{तत्}} \emph{tat}, which you will meet in a moment. The two of them differ by one sound at the front — \textbf{a-} for near — and that is not a coincidence. It is the whole system, and the last lesson of this chapter says so.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\sk{एतत्}\textquotedblright{} three times, pointing at something different each time
  \item it once with a word you already know after it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{etat}? (this one — the thing near me.) What sound does it start with, and does that sound mean near, far, or a question? (\textbf{a-} — near.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭa]{\sk{ट} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S116-letter-tta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{ए} · \sk{ठ} · \sk{ध}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ट}}
\textbf{\sk{ट}} — \emph{ṭa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ṭ}, it is \textbf{ṭa}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a descending central stem joined to a counterclockwise open round body
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say this word, and \sk{ट} is one of the shapes inside it — the rest of its shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kuṭumbam} — family, household — a word Sanskrit itself borrowed, before other languages borrowed it back
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ट}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the central stem's headline junction, descend, turn left through the upper shoulder, and sweep counterclockwise around the open round body to its up-right tip without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.} The pen comes up 1 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified two-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{ट}-order.gif’, strokes 1–2, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{ट} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{ट}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ट} three times, saying \emph{ṭa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{ट} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{ट}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ṭa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[la]{\sk{ल} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S213-letter-la}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{ठ} · \sk{ध} · \sk{ट}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ल}}
\textbf{\sk{ल}} — \emph{la}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{l}, it is \textbf{la}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a clockwise open left loop
  \item an up-right diagonal arm
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{ल} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{लिखति}} \emph{likhati} — he, she, or it writes — a root that means \textquotedblleft{}scratch,\textquotedblright{} and the chapter's four verbs gathered up
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ल}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the open lower-left tip, curve up and clockwise around the left loop, and finish at the inner junction
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at that junction and sweep the diagonal arm up-right to the right stem
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified four-stroke teaching form; another animated learner source writes the same parts in a stem-first order
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{ल}-order.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 11 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{ल} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{लिखति}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ल} three times, saying \emph{la} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{ल} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[o]{\sk{◌ो} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S214-vowel-sign-o}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{ध} · \sk{ट} · \sk{ल}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{◌ो}}
\textbf{\sk{◌ो}} — \emph{o}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Where it sits: the ā bar on the right plus a stroke above.

Worked through: \textbf{\sk{न}} + \textbf{\sk{◌ो}} = \textbf{\sk{नो}} — \emph{no}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{◌ो} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{करोमि}} \emph{karomi} — I do, I make
  \item \textbf{\sk{साहाय्यं} \sk{करोति}} \emph{sāhāyyaṁ karoti} — he, she, or it helps — a noun plus \textquotedblleft{}does,\textquotedblright{} and help named as going along with someone
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{◌ो} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \sk{◌ो} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{◌ो} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{करोमि}  ·  \sk{साहाय्यं} \sk{करोति}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{◌ो} three times, saying \emph{o} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{◌ो} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{◌ो}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{o} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[a- / t- / k-]{a- / t- / k- — six words, one machine}

\label{lesson:SA-C14-deixis-system}



\begin{quote}
Say the six words from this chapter out loud, in order. Listen to how they begin.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: one slot changes}]
You did not learn six words. You learned \textbf{three beginnings} and reused them.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{meaning} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
near & \textbf{\sk{अत्र}} \emph{atra} \\
far & \textbf{\sk{तत्र}} \emph{tatra} \\
question & \textbf{\sk{कुत्र}} \emph{kutra} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Sanskrit is where Hindi's k- comes from: \sk{अत्र}, \sk{तत्र}, \sk{कुत्र}.

Change the front, and the meaning walks from \textbf{near} to \textbf{far} to \textbf{a question}. Nothing else in the word moves.

The same three beginnings run the thing-words too: \textbf{\sk{एतत्}} \emph{etat} and \textbf{\sk{तत्}} \emph{tat} start exactly like the first two rows. This chapter did not teach you the matching question word for things — that one arrives later, and when it does you will already know what it has to start with.

This is worth more than the six words are. When you meet a new word in this family later, you will not have to be taught all three of it — you will be taught one and work out the others.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the near word, then the far word, then the question word
  \item \emph{Say it:} them again for place, not for things
  \item \emph{Notice:} the part that did NOT change
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which beginning means near? (\textbf{a-}) Far? (\textbf{t-}) And which one turns the word into a question? (\textbf{k-})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tha]{\sk{थ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S215-letter-tha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{ट} · \sk{ल} · \sk{◌ो}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{थ}}
\textbf{\sk{थ}} — \emph{tha}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{th}, it is \textbf{tha}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item an upper spiral joined continuously to a broad lower bowl
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{थ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{कथम्}} \emph{katham} — how
  \item \textbf{\sk{भवान्} \sk{कथम्} \sk{अस्ति}?} \emph{bhavān katham asti?} — how are you?
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{थ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the upper spiral's inner-right tip, curl clockwise around the small opening and outward to the left waist, then continue down and clockwise around the broad lower bowl to the right-stem junction without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

verified three-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{थ}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}
